name: StringZilla
workload: Find the first occurrence of a random ~5-byte word in text, measured as throughput (GB/s) on an Intel Xeon4 (Sapphire Rapids, GCC+glibc) and an Apple M5 Pro (Apple Clang+libc++).
claimed_speedup: std::string::find: 9.1 GB/s (Xeon4) / 10.9 GB/s (M5 Pro) vs StringZilla sz_find: 21.0 GB/s (Xeon4) / 37.1 GB/s (M5 Pro) -> ~2.3x faster on Xeon4, ~3.4x faster on M5 Pro (derived from page data). README also headlines '3x faster than LibC on Arm servers, 9x on Apple Silicon' for strstr/find.
compiler_and_flags: GCC + glibc on Xeon4 (Sapphire Rapids); Apple Clang + libc++ on M5 Pro. Exact optimization flags not printed in the README table; project builds with CMake/xmake, see bench/README.md for the underlying scripts.
hardware: Intel Xeon4 (Sapphire Rapids) and Apple M5 Pro (18-core Apple Silicon); an Nvidia H100 is also listed but not relevant to this CPU-only comparison.
tradeoffs: Header-only C core plus C++/Python/Rust/Go/Swift/JS/C#/Java bindings; adopting it means switching from std::string::find to sz::find/sz::string (a search-and-replace, per the README's own comparison table), not a drop-in override of std::string itself; portability across NEON/AVX2/AVX-512/SVE/RVV/WASM backends adds build-system complexity; its own hash function (AES-based) is a separate, non-standard hasher, not a std::hash specialization.
caveats: The README explicitly says 'Treat these as a first impression, not a benchmark suite.' The two CPUs differ in both ISA and standard library (glibc vs libc++), which the README itself flags as confounding part of the gap in the strstr/std::string::rfind rows. Numbers are first-party (project's own README), though methodology (compiler/stdlib/hardware) is stated for each column.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "stringzilla" (also surfaced via web search "substring search faster than std::string::find SIMD benchmark C++")

name: sse4-strstr (SIMD-friendly algorithms for substring searching)
baseline: std::strstr / libc strstr (same problem as std::string::find and the default std::search)
workload: Scan a fixed text corpus (data/i386.txt) for a word list (data/words) with SWAR/SSE2/SSE4.1/SSE4.2/AVX2 substring-search kernels vs std::strstr, timed end-to-end, on an Intel Skylake i7-6700 with GCC 5.4.1.
claimed_speedup: std::strstr: 0.662s vs AVX2 (generic) kernel: 0.364s -> ~1.82x faster (derived from page data); SSE2 (generic): 0.489s -> ~1.35x faster (derived from page data). Other machines in the results folder (Haswell, Cascade Lake, Knights Landing, ARMv7/ARMv8) show similar or larger gaps.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 5.4.1, -O3 -mavx2 (see FLAGS_AVX2 in the repo Makefile)
hardware: Intel Skylake i7-6700 (other result files cover Haswell i7-4770, Bulldozer FX-8510, Cascade Lake Gold 5217, Knights Landing 7210, Westmere, ARMv7/ARMv8)
tradeoffs: Companion code for a blog article (0x80.pl), not a packaged library -- integrating it means vendoring individual .cpp/.h kernels rather than linking a target; only exact single-needle substring search is covered (no wide-char, no custom predicates, no std::string_view-style API).
caveats: Repository unmaintained since Jan 2022 (~4.7 years); benchmarked hardware (Skylake, Haswell, etc.) predates several generations of CPUs and of glibc's own SIMD-optimized strstr, so the gap versus a current glibc/libstdc++ may be smaller today; the baseline is std::strstr (a C stdlib call reachable from C++ via <cstring>), not literally std::string::find or std::search, though it targets the identical substring-search primitive those two are built on.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "simd strstr"; author's site http://0x80.pl/articles/simd-strfind.html surfaced by web search

name: Boost.Algorithm Boyer-Moore / Boyer-Moore-Horspool searchers
workload: Locate an ~105 or ~43-character pattern (present in the middle/end, or absent) inside a 2,756,252-character random 8-bit text corpus, using boost::algorithm::boyer_moore_search / boyer_moore_horspool_search vs std::search, via the Boost.Algorithm search_test2 benchmark tool.
claimed_speedup: std::search: 0.4848s (100%, baseline) vs boyer_moore_search: 0.1171s (24.16%) vs boyer_moore_horspool_search: 0.1076s (22.2%) for a 105-char pattern found mid-corpus -- i.e. boyer_moore ~4.1x faster, boyer_moore_horspool ~4.5x faster than std::search (derived from page data; percentages are verbatim from the PR). A second case (91-char 'not found' pattern) shows std::search 1.028s vs boyer_moore_horspool 0.1825s (~5.6x, derived from page data).
stars_or_usage: 131 stars; boyer_moore_search/boyer_moore_horspool_search ship in mainline Boost.Algorithm and are used wherever Boost is deployed
tradeoffs: Boyer-Moore/Horspool searchers build an O(alphabet + pattern) skip table before searching, which pays off when reused or on longer patterns but adds overhead for a single tiny one-off search; since C++17 the same two algorithms are also standardized as std::boyer_moore_searcher / std::boyer_moore_horspool_searcher, usable directly with std::search -- so on a C++17+ toolchain the standard library itself can close most of this gap without Boost.
caveats: The quoted numbers come from Marshall Clow's (Boost.Algorithm's maintainer) still-open, unmerged PR #25 (from 2016, proposing an additional Musser-Nishanov searcher); the timing table is for the already-mainline boyer_moore/boyer_moore_horspool searchers, not the unmerged musser_nishanov code. Compiler, flags, and CPU model are not stated in the PR, so treat the ~4-5x figures as indicative rather than reproducible as-is; the author notes run-to-run variance of 5-10%.
found_via: WebSearch: "faster than std::search" OR "beats std::search" C++ benchmark github -> github.com/boostorg/algorithm/pull/25

name: komihash
workload: Hash short keys (0-15 bytes, 8-28 bytes) and 256,000-byte bulk buffers, averaged across 10 compiler/CPU combinations (GCC 11.5, Clang 18/19, ICC 19, clang-cl 18, Apple Clang 15) on Ryzen 3700X/9950X, Xeon E-2386G, Core i7-7700K, and Apple M1, measuring cycles/hash and GB/s.
claimed_speedup: Averaged over all 10 combos: komihash 5.34 needs ~7.2 cycles/hash (0-15b) and ~8.6 cycles/hash (8-28b) vs wyhash_final4's 13.5/18.0 and XXH3_64's 14.2/21.8 -- roughly 1.9-2x fewer cycles on short keys (derived from page data). On 256KB bulk hashing the result is mixed: komihash reaches up to 42.7 GB/s but XXH3_64 reaches up to 68.4 GB/s on some platforms, so komihash's advantage is specific to short/medium keys, not bulk throughput.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11.5.0 (-O3 -msse2 / -O3 -mavx2), LLVM Clang 19.1.7 (-O3 -mavx2), clang-cl 18.1.8 (/Ox -msse2 or -mavx2), ICC 19.0 (/O3 /QxSSE2), Apple Clang 15.0.0 (-O3) -- full 10-combo matrix given in the README
hardware: AMD Ryzen 3700X (4.2GHz) and Ryzen 9950X (5.7GHz), Intel Xeon E-2386G (5.1GHz), Core i7-7700K (4.5GHz), Apple M1 (3.5GHz)
tradeoffs: Non-cryptographic hash, not adversarial-collision-resistant without seeding; header-only C (compiles as C++) but exposes plain C functions (komihash(), komirand()) rather than a std::hash<T> specialization, so it needs a small wrapper to drop into unordered_map/unordered_set.
caveats: Never benchmarked against std::hash itself -- std::hash for strings in libstdc++/libc++ is a different, generally weaker-quality hash, so this evidence is against best-in-class non-cryptographic hashes (xxHash, wyhash), not literally the requested std::hash baseline. Numbers are the author's own benchmark (first-party), though the methodology (10 compiler/CPU combinations, exact flags) is unusually complete for a first-party result.

name: HighwayHash
workload: Hash inputs of 8, 31, 32, 63, 64, and 1024 bytes on a single idle core of a Xeon E5-2690 v3 (2.6GHz), comparing HighwayHashAVX2/SSE41 against SipHash, SipHash13, SipTreeHash and SipTreeHash13, measured in cycles/byte with a custom cycle-accurate nanobenchmark harness.
claimed_speedup: At 1024 bytes: HighwayHashAVX2 0.24 cycles/byte vs SipHash 1.26 cycles/byte -> ~5.25x faster (derived from page data, matching the README's own '5x faster' claim); at 64 bytes: HighwayHashAVX2 0.95 vs SipHash 1.93 -> ~2x faster (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: A patched GCC 4.9, 64-bit build (per README's 'Speed measurements' section)
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2690 v3, 2.6 GHz, single idle core
tradeoffs: SIMD-dependent (AVX2/SSE4.1/VSX), needs runtime CPU dispatch for portability; the hash output is explicitly declared 'frozen forever' so no further algorithmic improvements will ever land; repository is archived by Google (read-only) so no future compiler/security fixes.
caveats: Compared against SipHash/SipTreeHash, not std::hash. Benchmark used a 'patched' GCC 4.9 (a roughly decade-old, non-stock compiler) on hardware from ~2014-2015, and Google archived the repository in 2024, so these numbers do not reflect modern compilers or CPUs.

name: t1ha (Fast Positive Hash)
baseline: xxHash32 and the Murmur2/Murmur3 family (via the project's SMHasher-derived benchmark)
workload: Hash small keys (1-31 bytes) with t1ha's own SMHasher-derived benchmark tool on an Intel Core i7-6700K, comparing t1ha / t1ha_aes against xxHash32, Murmur2/2A/2B/2C/3F, FNV1a, CRC32/64-HW, MUM, and others, measured in MiB/s and cycles/hash.
claimed_speedup: t1ha_aes: 34,636 MiB/s (33.03 cycles/hash) and t1ha: 12,229 MiB/s (35.55 cycles/hash) vs xxHash32: 5,514 MiB/s (43.72 cycles/hash) -- i.e. t1ha_aes ~6.3x, t1ha ~2.2x higher throughput than xxHash32 on small keys (derived from page data).
tradeoffs: t1ha_aes variant is non-portable (requires AES-NI); several other variants (t1ha_32le/be) are explicitly flagged by the author as 'alien' -- designed for niche 32-bit or big-endian targets, not general-purpose use; t1ha0 dispatches to the fastest available implementation at runtime, adding a small indirection cost.
caveats: Benchmark data is from 2016 on a now decade-old CPU (Skylake i7-6700K) with GCC 5.4 -- results on current hardware/compilers may differ. Repository is archived, and the README notes the canonical GitHub repo was at one point removed and mirrored elsewhere, so provenance/continuity is a minor concern. Compares against xxHash32/Murmur, not std::hash directly.
